answer: You can address any [[Identity]] with `@name`, and any name is valid, so nothing needs to be declared first: mentioning `@sales` makes `sales` a known identity. Names can contain dots and are kept whole, so `@pete.smith` and `@sam.rivera` are each one mention (but no spaces).

--- Recipient.md ---
The Mention Inbox | description
An identity addressed with @name, whose mentions appear in the Mention Inbox.

--- Recipient.md ---
The Mention Inbox
A **recipient** is an [[Identity]] you address. When mentioned with `@name`, it is indexed to be queried, and clicking it in the editor will open the “Mentions Inbox”.

See [[At-Mention]] for the `@name` syntax, and [[Identity]] for where names come from (accounts, `identity.define`, or simply being mentioned).

--- Recipient.md ---
The Mention Inbox | Querying mentions
At-mentions are indexed like any other [[Object Index|relation]], with `kind == "at-mention"`. `to` is always the `@name` identifier (`toTag == "identity"`) and `alias` holds the name as typed. Build your own view over them with SLIQ, for example @sam.rivera:

${query[[
  from index.relations "at-mention"
  where _.to == "@sam.rivera"
  select { page = _.page, snippet = _.snippet }
]]}

Frontmatter declarations are relations too, with `kind == "recipients"`.

For a complete request, reply and resolution workflow, see [[Guide/Comments, Mentions and Replies]].

--- At-Mention.md ---
`@name` syntax | `@name` syntax
Type `@` followed by a name with no spaces, e.g. @jo. While typing, autocomplete offers every known identity.

A name may contain dots, so dotted usernames carry whole: @pete.smith and @sam.rivera are each one mention.

**Any name is a valid mention.** Nothing needs declaring up front: mentioning @sales makes `sales` a known identity. See [[Identity]] for more info.

For a complete request, reply and resolution workflow, see [[Guide/Comments, Mentions and Replies]].

--- At-Mention.md ---
`@name` syntax
An **at-mention** is the `@name` span you type in text. It refers to an [[Identity]], and it has two directions: written plainly it *addresses* that identity, making it a [[Recipient]], or when used as a signature it *credits* that identity instead, see [[Authorship]].
